lines.text: On the bench last time, a request that stayed on the motor after you let go was the problem. Now your code sends the request you already ran in Tuner X, and staying becomes useful.
That Control drop-down was picking a control request the whole time. The class in Java carries the same name, so there's nothing new to learn here. One field gets swapped.
Here's the swap. The old field named a voltage. This one names a target angle, and the motor works out the smooth ramp that gets the arm there.
The commands change with it. The two that pushed volts become two that each name a place, and the stop stays, because you may still want out partway through a move.
Each command is a single line. It says where the arm should be, in rotations, and it never finishes, so it keeps asking for that spot for as long as it runs.
Down here is where the target reaches the motor. The number goes into the request, and the request goes out.
Then the binding. The trigger starts the new command, and the piece that stopped the arm on release comes out.
This is last lesson's surprise turned around. Canceling still sends the motor nothing, so the last request stays, only now it's a place to hold and not a push that never ends.
Run it on the bench and watch two things. The arm stops at vertical by itself however long you hold, and it's still there after you let go.
If nothing moves at all, the values in your config are probably still zero, so paste it in again. Overshooting and hunting is a tuning problem, and that gets fixed in Tuner X.
Both new commands name a target and never finish. Nothing in the code can tell yet when the arm has arrived, and a routine will need to know.
